samples.text:
Social media is used by billions of people every day, and some of the content on it is harmful, such as fake news or hate speech. Some people think social media companies should be responsible for this content, while others believe the users who post it should be responsible. I will discuss both views in this essay.

On the one hand, there are reasons to blame social media companies. These companies earn a huge amount of money from advertisements, and they design their platforms to keep people online as long as possible. Sometimes shocking or false posts get more attention, so the companies do not have strong reason to remove them. Also, they have the technology and money to check content and delete harmful posts quickly. If they are responsible by law, they will work harder to protect users, especially children.

On the other hand, many people think the users should be responsible. The person who write a post decides what to say, so it is their fault if the post is harmful or untrue. Every day millions of posts are uploaded, and it is impossible for companies to check all of them. In addition, if companies have to delete many posts, they may also delete normal opinions, and this can reduce the freedom of speech.

In my opinion, both the companies and the users should have responsibility. Users must think carefully before they post something and they should be punished if they break the law. However, companies must also remove dangerous content fastly when people report it.

In conclusion, there are good arguments on both sides. I believe that the responsibility should be shared between social media companies and the users, because both of them can make internet safer.

samples.text:
The spread of harmful material online, from false information to abusive messages, has raised the question of who should be held accountable. Some argue that social media companies should be responsible for everything that appears on their platforms, while others believe the responsibility lies with the individuals who post it. In my view, both share responsibility, but companies should be held to a higher standard than they currently are.

Those who blame individual users make a straightforward argument. The person who writes a post chooses its content, so they should face the consequences if it is defamatory, threatening or illegal. It is also argued that the sheer volume of material uploaded every minute makes it impossible for any company to review everything. Furthermore, if platforms were legally liable for all content, they might remove anything controversial to protect themselves, which could seriously limit freedom of expression.

However, there are strong reasons to place significant responsibility on the companies themselves. Social media platforms are not neutral spaces; their algorithms decide which posts are promoted, and content that provokes strong emotions is often spread most widely because it generates more engagement and advertising revenue. In addition, these firms are extremely wealthy and have the technical ability to detect and remove harmful material far more effectively than they do at present. Many users also post anonymously, so holding individuals accountable are often difficult in practice.

I believe the responsibility should be shared. Users who break the law online should face the same penalties as they would offline, but companies should be required to act quickly when harmful content is reported and to be transparent about how their algorithms work.

In conclusion, while individual users remain responsible for what they post, social media companies profit from and amplify this content, and therefore they should also be held accountable for it.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · both views extended and well supported · logical organisation with a clear central idea per paragraph · good collocations (legally liable, freedom of expression) · mostly error-free with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
As social media has become a primary source of news and communication for many people, concern about harmful content, including misinformation, harassment and extremist material, has intensified. Some argue that the companies operating these platforms should be held responsible for what appears on them, while others insist that accountability lies with the individuals who post it. In my view, responsibility must be shared, but the role of the platforms has been significantly underestimated.

The case for holding users responsible rests on a basic principle of personal accountability. Each post is written by an individual who chooses its content, and it would seem perverse to excuse someone who spreads defamatory or threatening material simply because they did so online. There are also practical objections to placing the burden on companies. The volume of content uploaded every day is so vast that comprehensive monitoring is impossible, and platforms facing legal liability might respond by removing anything remotely contentious, with damaging consequences for free expression.

However, this view overlooks the active role that platforms play. They are not passive noticeboards: their recommendation systems determine what users see, and because provocative content tends to generate engagement, it is often amplified far beyond its original audience. Since these companies profit directly from this engagement, it is difficult to argue that they bear no responsibility for its effects. They also possess resources and technical expertise that no individual user could match, and anonymity frequently makes it impossible to identify the original author at all.

For these reasons, I believe a system of shared accountability is most appropriate. Individuals should face legal consequences for unlawful content, just as they would offline, while platforms should be obliged to respond promptly to reported material, limit the promotion of harmful posts and be transparent about how their algorithms operate.

In conclusion, although users are responsible for the content they create, social media companies shape and profit from its distribution, and they should therefore be held accountable for the part they play.
samples.why: Both views thoroughly developed and critically evaluated · clear, nuanced position · logical progression and skilful cohesion · wide, precise vocabulary (perverse, amplified, recommendation systems) · wide range of accurate complex structures.
